title: going to - intentions and obvious predictions
shortExplanation: I'm going to visit Paris. Look out - you're going to fall!
longExplanation:
going to is used for:
1. Pre-made decisions and intentions: I'm going to start a diet next week.
2. Predictions with visible signs: Look at those clouds - it's going to rain!
Form: am/is/are + going to + infinitive
formation: I'm going to visit Paris. Look out - you're going to fall!

examples.sentence: I'm going to study medicine.
examples.translation: I'm going to study medicine.

examples.sentence: She's going to have a baby.
examples.translation: She's expecting a baby.

title: Present Continuous: am/is/are + V-ing
shortExplanation: She is reading now. They are playing outside.
longExplanation:
Present Continuous is an action taking place right now or temporarily during this period.
Form: am/is/are + verb + -ing
Rules for writing -ing:
• Most: just + ing → working, playing
• Ends with -e: remove -e + ing → making, coming
• Short stressed syllable: double the last consonant → running, sitting
formation: She is reading now. They are playing outside.

examples.sentence: I am studying English right now.
examples.translation: I'm studying English now.

examples.sentence: She's working from home this month.
examples.translation: She is working from home this month.

title: Present Continuous for planned future
shortExplanation: I'm meeting Tom tomorrow. We're flying to Rome on Friday.
longExplanation:
Present Continuous is used for specific agreements in the future - when the time and place have already been determined.
Difference:
• I'm meeting Alice tomorrow - the meeting has been agreed (a specific plan)
• I'll meet Alice tomorrow - intention or proposal
formation: I'm meeting Tom tomorrow. We're flying to Rome on Friday.

examples.sentence: I'm having dinner with Alex tonight.
examples.translation: I'm having dinner with Alex tonight.

examples.sentence: They're getting married in June.
examples.translation: They are getting married in June.

title: Present Simple vs Present Continuous - difference
shortExplanation: I drink coffee (habit) vs I am drinking coffee (right now)
longExplanation:
Present Simple: habits, facts, schedules, general truths.
Present Continuous: something that is happening right now or temporarily.
Compare:
• She speaks French. - knows the language (always)
• She is speaking French. - speaks right now
formation: I drink coffee (habit) vs I am drinking coffee (right now)

examples.sentence: Water boils at 100°C. (факт)
examples.translation: Water boils at 100°C.

examples.sentence: I'm reading a great book this week. (временно)
examples.translation: I'm reading a great book this week.

title: should / shouldn't - advice and recommendation
shortExplanation: You should see a doctor. You shouldn't eat so much.
longExplanation:
should expresses mild advice or personal opinion. Weaker than must.
After should - infinitive without to.
Also used for criticism or regret: You should have called (should have called).
formation: You should see a doctor. You shouldn't eat so much.

examples.sentence: You should exercise more.
examples.translation: You should exercise more.

examples.sentence: She shouldn't work so hard.
examples.translation: She shouldn't work so hard.

title: must / mustn't - obligation and strict prohibition
shortExplanation: You must wear a seatbelt. You mustn't smoke here.
longExplanation:
must - a strong obligation (often internal) or a categorical requirement.
mustn't - a strict prohibition (absolutely impossible!).
• mustn't = prohibited
• don't have to = not required, but possible
formation: You must wear a seatbelt. You mustn't smoke here.

examples.sentence: You must show your passport.
examples.translation: You must present your passport.

examples.sentence: You mustn't smoke here.
examples.translation: You can't smoke here.

title: have to - external necessity
shortExplanation: I have to work late. She doesn't have to come.
longExplanation:
have to - a necessity due to external rules, circumstances or other people's requirements.
Difference from must:
• must - internal necessity: I must call her (I myself consider it necessary)
• have to - external: I have to wear a uniform (rule)
don't have to=optional (not necessary, but allowed).
formation: I have to work late. She doesn't have to come.

examples.sentence: I have to finish this report by Friday.
examples.translation: I have to submit my report by Friday.

examples.sentence: You don't have to come if you don't want to.
examples.translation: You don't have to come.

title: could - past skill and polite requests
shortExplanation: She could swim when she was 5. Could you help me?
longExplanation:
could is the past tense of can. Two main meanings:
1. Skill in the past: I could read at 4 years old.
2. Polite requests (more polite than can): Could you pass the salt, please?
Also for present possibility: It could be true.
formation: She could swim when she was 5. Could you help me?

examples.sentence: She could play the violin as a child.
examples.translation: She knew how to play the violin as a child.

examples.sentence: Could you speak more slowly, please?
examples.translation: Could you speak more slowly?

title: Comparative degree of adjectives
longExplanation:
Monosyllabic and disyllabic in -y: + er (fast→faster, happy→happier).
Polysyllabic: more + adjective.
Writing rules: -e → + r (nice→nicer); short stressed syllable: double (big→bigger); -y → ier (heavy→heavier).
Irregular: good→better, bad→worse, far→further/farther, much/many→more
After the comparative - than: She is taller than her sister.

examples.sentence: This film is more interesting than that one.
examples.translation: This movie is more interesting than that.

examples.sentence: Today is worse than yesterday.
examples.translation: Today is worse than yesterday.

title: Superlative adjectives
shortExplanation: the biggest, the most beautiful, the best
longExplanation:
Monosyllabic: the + -est. Polysyllabic: the most.
The writing rules are the same as for the comparative degree.
Irregular: good→the best, bad→the worst, far→the furthest, much/many→the most
formation: the biggest, the most beautiful, the best

examples.sentence: This is the most expensive restaurant in the city.
examples.translation: This is the most expensive restaurant in the city.

examples.sentence: He is the best player on the team.
examples.translation: He is the best player on the team.

title: some / any - indefinite amount
shortExplanation: I have some money. Do you have any? I don't have any.
longExplanation:
some - in affirmative sentences and in offers/requests.
any - in questions and negations.
Exception: some in questions when we expect an affirmative answer or offer something: Would you like some tea? Can I have some water?
formation: I have some money. Do you have any? I don't have any.

examples.sentence: I bought some bread and some milk.
examples.translation: I bought bread and milk.

examples.sentence: Is there any milk in the fridge?
examples.translation: Is there milk in the refrigerator?

examples.sentence: I don't have any cash on me.
examples.translation: I don't have cash with me.

pattern: much / many / a lot of / a few / a little
title: much / many / a lot of / a few / a little
shortExplanation: much water (uncountable), many people (countable), a lot of - everywhere
longExplanation:
much - with uncountables (much water, much time, much money).
many - with countables (many people, many books, many times).
a lot of / lots of - with both, conversational style.
a few - a little (countable, neutral/positive).
few - few, almost none (countable, negative).
a little - a little (uncountable, neutral).
little - little, almost none (uncountable, negative).
formation: much water (uncountable), many people (countable), a lot of - everywhere

examples.sentence: I don't have much time.
examples.translation: I don't have much time.

examples.sentence: She has a few friends in London.
examples.translation: She has several friends in London.

examples.sentence: There is a little sugar left.
examples.translation: There is some sugar left.

title: Countable and uncountable nouns
shortExplanation: water, information, advice - not allowed: a water, two advices
longExplanation:
Countable: you can count, there are plural. number: a book, two books.
Uncountable: cannot be counted directly - no plural. numbers, no indefinite article.
Typical uncountables: water, milk, bread, rice, money, information, advice, news, weather, luggage, furniture, hair, music, work
To indicate portions: a glass of water, a piece of advice, a loaf of bread, a bag of rice
formation: water, information, advice - not allowed: a water, two advices

examples.sentence: Can I have some information, please?
examples.translation: May I know something?

examples.sentence: She gave me very useful advice.
examples.translation: She gave me very useful advice.

pattern: Prepositions in / on / at for time
title: Prepositions in / on / at for time
shortExplanation: in March, in 2024, in winter; on Monday, on June 5; at 3pm, at night
longExplanation:
at → exact time: at 6 o'clock, at noon, at midnight, at night, at the weekend (BrE)
on → days and dates: on Monday, on 5 March, on my birthday, on New Year's Day
in → periods: in July, in 2023, in the morning/afternoon/evening, in summer, in the 21st century
Without preposition: this/last/next + time: this morning, last week, next year
formation: in March, in 2024, in winter; on Monday, on June 5; at 3pm, at night

examples.sentence: The meeting is at half past three.
examples.translation: Meeting at half past four.

examples.sentence: She was born on the 12th of April.
examples.translation: She was born on April 12.

examples.sentence: I started this job in October.
examples.translation: I started this work in October.

title: for / since / ago - duration and beginning
shortExplanation: for three years, since 2020, three years ago
longExplanation:
for - duration (how long): for two hours, for a week, for years. Used with different tenses.
since - initial moment (since): since Monday, since 2019, since I was a child. Used with the Present Perfect.
ago - time ago from now: three days ago, a month ago. Only with Past Simple.
formation: for three years, since 2020, three years ago

examples.sentence: I've been here for six months.
examples.translation: I've been here for six months now.

examples.sentence: She's worked here since 2020.
examples.translation: She has been working here since 2020.

examples.sentence: I saw him two days ago.
examples.translation: I saw him two days ago.
